title: What Is the Kerch Bridge—and Why Does Ukraine Keep Attacking It?
author: Tiago Ventura
body:
An overnight Ukrainian missile attack has severely damaged the vital Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia, delivering a symbolic blow to Russian President Vladimir Putin ahead of a summit in Asia where he is expected to meet President Donald Trump.

The road and rail bridge was built after Russia invaded and annexed the Crimean peninsula in 2014 and connects Crimea to Russia's southern Krasnodar region.

Ukrainian officials shared videos on social media that appeared to show a missile strike on the bridge and an entire section of the structure collapsing. TIME could not immediately verify the footage.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Tuesday morning that the overnight strikes served as a reminder to “Russia that war will always return to where it began.”

Sergei Aksyonov, the Russian-installed governor of Crimea, confirmed the Ukrainian strike and said traffic across the bridge had been suspended.

“Measures are being taken to restore transport links disrupted as a result of enemy attacks on the Crimean Bridge,” he said Tuesday on Telegram.

Ukraine's armed forces said the bridge's road arch had fallen into the Kerch Strait, which connects the Sea of Azov with the Black Sea, while the railway arch had also sustained damage.

“For the occupiers, this is more than a symbolic blow. The bridge was the main artery carrying fuel, ammunition, equipment and personnel to the peninsula and on into southern Ukraine,” the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine said, framing the attack as an effort to disrupt Russian military supply lines. “The occupiers are left with fewer and fewer land routes to Crimea. Every hour without traffic over the bridge means Russian groupings in the south receive less of what they need to keep fighting.”

Zelensky added that the attack was part of “an unprecedented operation in response to Russian strikes on our infrastructure.”

Russia has been ramping up its attacks on Ukraine's civilian and energy infrastructure as the country heads into the winter months, placing further pressure on Kyiv amid ongoing peace negotiations.

In the Ukrainian capital, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said Russian forces had struck two bridges spanning the Dnipro River and other infrastructure on Monday.

Officials in Kyiv also reported further strikes on the country's power grid across multiple regions, as cities throughout Ukraine faced water and electricity outages.

Ukraine, meanwhile, has intensified its own military pressure on Russia, with the attack on the Kerch Bridge coming amid the largest overnight Ukrainian drone barrage against Russia since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022. Russia's Defense Ministry confirmed it had shot down 1,441 drones across 22 regions.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Tuesday that Russian Deputy Prime Minister Marat Khusnullin had briefed Putin on the situation at the Crimean Bridge, according to Russian news agency Interfax. "There is no doubt that the bridge will be restored and will be even better than before,” Peskov added.

Why the Kerch bridge matters to Putin

The Kerch bridge, also known as the Crimean bridge, stretches roughly 19 km (12 miles) across the strait, providing a direct road and rail link between Crimea and Russia without the need to travel through mainland Ukraine.

Carlo Masala, a professor of security and defense policy at the Bundeswehr University Munich, describes it as one of “Putin's prestige projects after he annexed Crimea.”

“It's a highly symbolic and high value target for the Ukrainians to destroy the bridge," he tells TIME.

Putin personally drove the lead truck across the bridge when its road section opened in 2018 and also attended the launch of passenger rail services in 2019, underscoring the political importance he has placed on the crossing.

“Symbolically, the bridge is one of the clearest physical expressions of Moscow’s claim to Crimea,” Basil Germond, a professor of international security at Lancaster University, tells TIME.

Germond explains that the bridge “was intended to demonstrate that Crimea had been permanently integrated into Russia."

"Serious damage to such a prominent and heavily defended structure is therefore an embarrassing blow to the Kremlin," he says.

The bridge has repeatedly been targeted by Ukraine since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion. Ukrainian officials have previously described an attack involving explosives carried by a truck in 2022, attacks using naval surface drones in 2023, and a further operation involving underwater explosions in 2025.

Beyond its symbolic importance, experts tell TIME that the latest strike also demonstrates Ukraine's military capabilities and its ability to target Russian infrastructure.

“What Ukrainians showed is that they now have ballistic missiles which can hit targets in Russia very precisely within a reach of thousands of kilometers,” says Masala.

The damage could also have broader consequences for Russia, with the bridge serving as an important transport link for civilians traveling between Crimea and the Russian mainland.

“If the road crossing remains closed, this may also deepen the feeling among residents of Crimea that the peninsula is geographically vulnerable rather than securely connected to Russia. All that plays a part in diminishing morale among the Russian population,” explains Germond.

The disruption could also complicate Russian military supply lines, although Moscow has developed alternative routes to support its forces in southern Ukraine.

Germond says that “operationally, disruption to the road bridge will make Russian logistics more complicated and expensive.”

“Russia can still use the occupied land corridor through southern Ukraine, as well as ferries and other connections, but these alternatives are longer, less efficient and potentially more exposed to Ukrainian attack,” he adds.

The apparent obstruction of the shipping channel beneath the bridge could create an additional challenge for maritime traffic between the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov.

The strike has nevertheless been welcomed by some Ukrainian observers, who celebrated the long-awaited destruction of parts of the bridge. Serhii Sternenko, a former adviser to Ukraine's Defense Ministry, wrote on social media: “Ukraine destroyed [the] Crimean bridge. Just help Ukraine defeat Russia. We can do it.”

Still, experts caution that the destruction of the bridge is little more than symbolic.

“The strike does not in itself transform the balance of power or guarantee Ukraine a stronger negotiating position. It does, however, reinforce Kyiv’s argument that Ukraine is not a defeated or passive actor. Ukraine has demonstrated that it can penetrate Russian defenses, strike strategically and politically important infrastructure, and impose costs far beyond the immediate front line,” says Germond.

How could the strike affect Ukraine-Russia peace talks?

The latest blow to the Kremlin comes as Putin prepares to travel to China for a trilateral meeting with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Although the full agenda for the meeting remains unclear, Putin has previously indicated that it would include discussions on ending the war in Ukraine, with Trump telling reporters Monday that the topics would range from denuclearization to Iran and Ukraine.

“I think [Putin]’s backing down a little bit. I think he could be tougher. I think he could be a lot tougher,” Trump said, adding “I think he'd like to see it finished.”

Germond argues that the strike on Kerch is an important display of Ukraine's military capabilities ahead of the diplomatic summit, reinforcing Kyiv's position that it can continue to impose costs on Russia despite ongoing negotiations.

“Ukraine will want to persuade Trump and other international partners that continued support strengthens a capable actor that still has meaningful leverage. Kyiv’s message is that negotiations conducted under sustained pressure on Russia are more likely to produce results than negotiations based on the assumption that Russian military superiority is inevitable,” he says.

The ongoing peace efforts have been led by U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who met with Putin in Moscow last week before traveling to Ireland later that day to brief Zelensky on the developments.

Their visit followed two days of U.S.-mediated negotiations in Abu Dhabi between Russian and Ukrainian delegations. Those discussions ended without a major breakthrough, with significant differences remaining between the two sides.

Kushner confirmed Monday that the U.S. remained in communication with Ukrainian and European officials, with European representatives expected to be included in the next round of talks.

“Important challenges remain, and a final agreement will require difficult decisions. But we are making progress, in close coordination with Russia, Ukraine, and Europe, toward an outcome that can end this war, strengthen European security, and create the foundations for lasting peace,” he said.
